title: Chris Kelly's clarinetists and how blues were played
summary: Clarinetists in Kelly's band, their tone, and how clarinet, trombone and muted trumpet handled the blues.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: He was really great blues man. Who did Chris have in his band, if you'd say so?

Oh, I had George Lewis. At various times they would play together a while and Georgey Boy, certainly I, Neely Bones, at certain times they would have two jobs and split up. I saw him have jobs in using two clarinet players in the band. Do you remember who the two were? Yeah. We had Zeb, Neely, times like that, you know. Georgey Boy and George Lewis. Mostly it would be Tyne, like maybe perhaps he was short of a man, a trombone player, or either a bass player. It must have sounded good. It must have sounded good. It was good. It was, it was. They really played clarinet. All those guys, great clarinet. They really could get something out of them. Such nice tones, not like they did the tones that the new clarinet players, the young ones. And all of those guys played.
Albert's system, Albert's system, Albert's system, no Barum system.
Nowadays you can't catch a youngster. You'd have to count the one that you can find, can play an Albert's system, but they all played a Barum system.
What about those blues? Did the clarinet players specialize in blues much?

Oh yeah. That's what made it so great. The clarinet and trombone players, the way they would harmonize and make high notes and come down and low register and play. And finally the trumpet player you would take a solo and they would make stop time, what we would call after beats. And he would put mutes, his doily on his trumpet. And he would get a lot out of it without using the vowels on the trumpet. Real great. You couldn't imagine, I mean the difference, and today and at that time. Without using the vowels you said? Various notes could be made. Without using the vowels without you. You use it at your feelings. And something like Lewis. You ever see Lewis when he plays, he uses a towel over his horn all the time? He can make so many things with his lip that a fellow would think he's making some of that with his vowel. But you have to be good to do that. Some guy can't make it with the vowel, they're not making this with their lips. And that's a long time ago. The older musicians would always hide different things from another trumpet player. He didn't want them to catch on to his style. And that's why they would put their pocket handshake over their hand and like their finger, you couldn't see what he was fingering.
